blocks.heading: EVERYDAY EXPRESSION — “Peace be upon you / hello”

paragraphs: Each chapter begins with a common Arabic expression.

The idea behind this is simple: I want you to get used to the feel of the language, not just the structure of the language. Arabic is full of social expressions, greetings, blessings, and responses that carry respect, warmth, and connection.

This book can guide you, organize the grammar, and give you the tools. But real language learning also means learning how people actually speak and interact with each other. These chapter-opening expressions are one small way to help you start immersing yourself in the culture and rhythm of Arabic.
Let's start with one of the most important greetings:
You will hear is-salām ʿalēkum throughout the Arabic-speaking world. Literally, it means “peace be upon you,” but in everyday life it works much more like a warm and respectful hello.
Although ʿalēkum is grammatically plural, you do not need to be speaking to a group. The same greeting is commonly used with one person or with several people.

blocks.heading: Where you will use it
paragraphs: You can say is-salām ʿalēkum when entering a room, walking into a shop, greeting someone at home, or simply starting a conversation.

Although the phrase has Islamic roots, it is not used only by Muslims. In Jordan and Palestine, Muslims, Christians, and people from many backgrounds use it as part of ordinary everyday speech. You can use it in many everyday settings, and most people will immediately understand it and know how to respond.

blocks.heading: What’s Your Name? | شو اسمك؟ | shū ismak?
paragraphs: The fastest way to start speaking Levantine Arabic is simple: start speaking it right now.

That is why this first chapter begins with one of the most common questions in any language: “What’s your name?” Instead of making you wait through pages of grammar before you can say anything useful, we are going to begin with the everyday phrases and expressions you actually need when meeting people and introducing yourself.
I should warn you: I am going to drop you in the deep end a little.

From the beginning, you will see complete sentences and ready-made expressions before you fully understand how every part of them works. That is intentional. You are not expected to analyze every word, memorize every rule, or understand everything immediately.
For now, use the language first. The explanations will come.

Throughout this book, we will return to the grammar behind many of the expressions you meet early on. By the time you reach the end, in shāʾ Allāh, you will be able to look back at these first conversations and understand structures that initially felt unfamiliar.

If you already know Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), you will recognize a great deal. Levantine Arabic shares much of the same vocabulary, roots, and underlying structure, but everyday speech has its own pronunciation, rhythm, expressions, and grammatical patterns.
If you are starting completely from scratch, that is fine too. This chapter is designed to get you communicating before you have mastered all the rules.

At first, that may feel uncomfortable. Again, that is part of the process. This is not an exercise in rote memorization. The goal is to acclimate you to spoken Arabic—to get your ears used to hearing it and your mouth used to producing its sounds, rhythm, and patterns.
Listen. Repeat. Speak out loud.

Do not worry if you cannot explain the grammar yet. You will encounter these expressions and structures again throughout the book, and each time they will make a little more sense. What feels like a ready-made phrase today will eventually become a pattern you understand and can use to build your own sentences.
We begin with greetings, introductions, and common everyday expressions because these are your first survival tools. They will help you:
• break the ice
• ask and answer “What’s your name?” naturally
• respond comfortably in simple conversations
• begin sounding like a person having a conversation rather than someone reciting a textbook

These ready-made expressions are extremely valuable. Later, when the grammar becomes more challenging and the vocabulary starts piling up, you will still have useful language you can reach for immediately. That keeps you communicating while everything else is still falling into place.
From there, we will begin adding the essential building blocks—pronouns, question words, and a few key structures—and gradually show you how the language you have already been using actually works.
You may be surprised how quickly you can go from:
“Hello. What’s your name?”
to having short, real conversations in Levantine Arabic.
Ready? Let’s dive in.

blocks.heading: 1.1 Greetings & Basics
paragraphs: We are going to start with some of the most common greetings, responses, and basic expressions you will hear in everyday Arabic.

Many of these phrases are fixed expressions. That means someone says one phrase, and the response is usually already known. They really only change with respect to who is speaking and who is being spoken to, and those changes are minor. This is great for you as a student because you do not have to build every response from scratch. You can learn the whole exchange as one unit and use it right away.
You may also notice a kind of "one-up" pattern in Arabic greetings. Someone gives you a warm phrase, and the response often gives back something even warmer. For example:
The normal response is:

So the response is not just a repeat. Someone gives you goodness, and you give them back light. This pattern reflects something important about Arabic-speaking culture. Greetings are not just practical. They create warmth, respect, optimism, and connection before the real conversation even begins. You will see this again and again. Someone welcomes you, and you welcome them back. Someone wishes you goodness, and you return light. Someone thanks you, and you respond with something generous.
For now, do not overanalyze every word inside these expressions. Learn them as complete phrases. Say them out loud. Practice the response. Get used to the rhythm.
Many greetings in Arabic come as pairs: one person begins the exchange, and the other gives the expected response.
Do not worry about analyzing every word yet. Learn the two sides together.
Say the greeting.
• Say the response.
• Reverse roles.
• Repeat the exchange several times aloud.
The goal is for the response to begin coming automatically when you hear the greeting.

These expressions are reliable tools. When your mind feels overloaded, or when you just want to sound natural, they give you something solid to fall back on. Practice them out loud and practice them often.

Over time, these phrases will start to feel automatic. That is exactly what you want. The more natural they feel, the more you will begin to feel the warmth and rhythm of everyday Levantine communication.

blocks.heading: Speaking About Yourself
paragraphs: There is one more basic idea you should know before we move into greetings.
When you describe yourself in Arabic, the word describing you may change depending on whether you are a man or a woman.
Strictly speaking, Arabic also pays attention to number—whether we are talking about one person or more than one—but we will save that for later.
For now, just focus on gender.
Notice that أَنَا stays exactly the same.
What changes is the word describing the speaker:
In short, when a man answers the question “How are you?”, he uses the masculine form without an additional ending. When a woman answers, she uses the feminine form, which ends with a tāʾ marbūṭa (ة).
I just want you to start noticing the pattern, because you will see it again as soon as we begin learning basic greetings.
For example:
That is all you need for now.
The goal is simply to notice that describing words change depending on who is speaking.

We will build on all of this as we move into greetings and everyday expressions. On the next page, you will meet your first vocabulary bank. Most of the items there are best treated, for now, as fixed expressions—useful phrases you can learn and start using right away without worrying about every piece of grammar inside them.

There's a lot of vocabulary here, but don't worry about memorizing it all right away. Use these pages as a reference, and practice speaking the expressions aloud, paying attention to their natural rhythm and flow.

blocks.heading: Basics & Greetings Discussion
paragraphs: Before we move on, there are two things I want you to keep in mind about the greetings and expressions you just saw.

First, the responses in the vocabulary bank are not the only possible answers. I included a wide range of expressions so that you could begin seeing different ways people greet each other, respond, and keep a conversation moving.
For many general questions that basically mean “How are you?”, “How are things?”, or “What’s new?”, the same kinds of responses can often work across the board.
For example:
These can all work naturally in response to a number of everyday “How are you?” type questions.
So do not think of the vocabulary bank as a list where each question has only one correct answer. Real conversation is much more flexible than that.
The purpose of this vocabulary bank is to give you a broad range of useful expressions and help you begin recognizing how basic Levantine conversations are put together.
And yes, there is a lot here.
You are not expected to memorize all of it right now. At this stage, simply become familiar with the expressions and start noticing which ones you recognize when you see or hear them again.
Think of these pages as a reference you can return to throughout the chapter and the rest of the book.
On the next page, we will look at a simple method for practicing these expressions so that they begin to feel more natural in real conversation.

blocks.title: Speaker-Responder Drill
blocks.instructions:
Instructions: This drill is designed to help you become comfortable with the rhythm and flow of everyday Levantine Arabic. You will practice common greetings, expressions, and their natural responses. This is not a test, and you are not expected to memorize everything immediately.

For now, focus on understanding the general meaning of each expression, when to use it, and how it sounds as a complete phrase. Rather than concentrating on the meaning of every individual word, pay attention to how the sounds connect, where the natural emphasis falls, and how one part of the expression flows into the next. Think of it almost like learning the rhythm of a song.

Using a metronome can be especially helpful. You can download a free metronome app on your phone or use one online. Start with a comfortable, steady beat and practice speaking the expressions along with it. The goal is not to force every syllable onto a beat, but to develop a natural, consistent rhythm. A metronome is optional, but I strongly recommend trying one.

Say every Arabic line out loud, including those marked SOFT. Say the LOUD lines in a clear, confident voice and the SOFT lines more quietly. Soft does not mean silently. As you switch between the two, try to maintain the natural rhythm of each expression.

If you are working with a tutor or partner, divide the Speaker and Responder roles between you, then switch. If you are practicing alone, play both roles yourself.

Whenever several options appear after a slash, practice every option. Repeat each exchange several times, paying attention to pronunciation, rhythm, and how the expression and its response fit together.

Remember, the goal right now is to get your ears and mouth accustomed to the sound of Arabic, not to analyze every word. The more you practice these expressions as complete units, the more naturally they will come to you in real conversations.

blocks.heading: 1.2 Interrogatives: Question Words
paragraphs: You’ve already been using some question words.
For example:
So far, we’ve been treating these as complete expressions. Now we’re going to take a closer look inside them and focus on the individual words that make these questions work.
Grammatically, question words are called interrogatives. An interrogative is simply a word used to ask for information.
In English, you use them every day:
Who is that?
What is this?
Where are we?
When does it start?
Why did that happen?
How do you do that?

Who, what, where, when, why, and how—these are the main interrogatives we use in English. Arabic generally works the same way, though it also has a separate interrogative for “how much” or “how many.” You will meet that one below.

Once you learn these words in Arabic, you’ll start noticing them in conversations all the time. More importantly, you’ll begin to see how questions are built instead of having to memorize each one as a complete expression.

I always encourage my students to ask as many questions as they can—and to ask them in as many different ways as they can. Questions are one of the most useful tools you have when learning a language. Every question gives you another opportunity to hear new words, notice patterns, and better understand how the language works.
Let’s begin with the interrogatives you’ll use most often.

blocks.heading: Levantine Interrogatives
paragraphs: Some of these words may look familiar if you’ve studied Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). When helpful, you’ll see brief notes showing how they relate. If you’re starting with dialect, you can safely ignore those—focus on how the words are used in everyday speech.

items.notes: Used to ask about the identity of a person. Word origin: Derived from the older Arabic مَن (man), meaning “who?” The pronunciation changed over time, but the word retains the same meaning.

The most common everyday way to ask about things, information, or descriptions. Word origin: Historically connected to older Arabic expressions involving شيء (shayʾ), meaning “thing.” It developed into the short everyday interrogative شو and is not simply a spoken pronunciation of MSA ماذا (mādhā).

Another common word for “what?” especially in Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic. It is generally interchangeable with شو in these examples. Word origin: Developed from the older Arabic expression أيّ شيء (ayy shayʾ), literally meaning “which thing?” Over time, the expression shortened into إيش.
Used to ask about the location of a person, place, or thing. Word origin: Related historically to the older Arabic أين (ʾayna), meaning “where?” The everyday Levantine form is وين (wēn).

Used to ask about the time or date of an event. Word origin: Derived from the older Arabic متى (matā), meaning “when?” The Levantine form developed a different vowel pattern while preserving the original meaning.

Used to ask for a reason or explanation. Word origin: Formed from لـ (li-), meaning “for,” and إيش (ēsh), meaning “what?” Together, they express the idea of “for what?” or “what for?” The two elements eventually combined into ليش (lēsh).

Used to ask about the way something is. Word origin: Derived from كيف (kayfa), meaning “how?” The Levantine pronunciation became kīf, dropping the final vowel and changing the vowel sound, while retaining the original meaning.

blocks.heading: How much? / How many? — ʾaddēsh / qaddēsh | قدّيش

items.notes: Used to ask about prices, amounts, quantities, measurements, numbers, and current time. Word origin: قدّيش developed from combining قدّ (qadd), meaning “amount,” “size,” or “extent,” with إيش (ēsh), meaning “what?” Together, they express the idea of “what amount?” or “to what extent?” In everyday Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic, the ق is often pronounced as a glottal stop (ʾ), giving us ʾaddēsh.

items.note: Suspected source issue: this example under قدّيش uses كم (kam), which is not otherwise introduced.

items.notes: Used to pick one out of several. Word origin: Same word as Standard Arabic أيّ (ayy), “which?” The word has remained essentially unchanged in Levantine Arabic.

blocks.heading: 1.3 Pronouns & Names
paragraphs: The next thing we need is pronouns—words like I, you, he, she, we, and they. They might look simple, but they are among the most important words in the language.

A pronoun is a word that stands in for a noun or noun phrase, allowing us to avoid repeating names and helping language flow more naturally. In other words, instead of saying Layla is tired because Layla didn’t sleep, we can say Layla is tired because she didn’t sleep. The pronoun she replaces the second Layla, keeping the sentence clear and smooth.

In Arabic, once you know your pronouns, you can already begin making complete sentences. At first, a pronoun can simply be paired with a name, and later with nouns, adjectives, and eventually verbs. Learning these few words gives you an essential foundation for almost everything that follows.

blocks.heading: A Quick Note
blocks.text:
Arabic does not use one single pronoun equivalent to English it. Instead, the pronoun normally matches the grammatical gender of the noun. Therefore, we use هو (huwwe) and هي (hiyye) for both people and things. Likewise, هم (humme) can refer to groups of people or groups of things.

Don’t worry about why one thing uses هو and another uses هي just yet. In the next chapter, you’ll begin learning nouns and discover that Arabic nouns belong to one of two grammatical groups. For now, simply remember that هو and هي can also mean it.

paragraphs: Arabic is a very formulaic language, so throughout this book, we’ll build new skills by learning simple formulas and expanding them one step at a time. There is one more important thing to notice: in these basic Arabic sentences, we are not going to use a separate word for “am,” “is,” or “are.” Arabic can simply place the pronoun and the name next to each other and form a complete sentence.
We’ll explore this much more in the next chapter, so don’t worry about understanding the whole rule yet. Right now, we’re just getting the wheels turning.

items.en: It is a Mercedes (i.e. the car).

paragraphs: For now, focus on recognizing the pronouns and getting comfortable with the rhythm of these simple sentences.

blocks.heading: How to Learn the Pronouns
paragraphs: The pronouns may look like a long list at first, but they are actually organized into three simple groups: the person speaking, the person being spoken to, and the person or thing being spoken about.
Learning them in these groups gives your brain much less work to do.
Both ana and iḥna contain the sound -na. That shared sound can help you recognize that they belong together.
To remember ana, imagine that Ana is a person’s name:
“I am Ana.”
Then remember that iḥna means we.
Practice them together: ana, iḥna | أنا، إحنا — I, we
As you say ana, point to yourself. As you say iḥna, make a circle with your hand that includes yourself and other people.

blocks.heading: Second Person: The Person You Are Speaking To

paragraphs: All three second-person pronouns share the sound int-. As soon as you hear that sound, you already know that the speaker is addressing you.
Only the ending changes:
inta — you, speaking to one male
intī — you, speaking to one female
intu — you, speaking to more than one person
This gives you much less to memorize. First, listen for int-. Then listen to the ending to determine whether the speaker is addressing a male, a female, or a group.
Practice them together: inta, intī, intu | إنتَ، إنتي، إنتو — you, you(f.), you(pl.)

As you practice, imagine pointing to one man when you say inta, one woman when you say intī, and a group of people when you say intu. For the plural, you can sweep your hand across an imaginary group.

blocks.heading: Third Person: The Person or Thing Being Spoken About

paragraphs: All three third-person pronouns begin with an h sound. When you hear that sound, you have an immediate clue that the speaker is talking about someone or something rather than speaking directly to them. Then listen to the rest of the word:
huwwe — he or it
hiyye — she or it
humme — they
To remember huwwe, connect it with the English question:
“Who is he?” — huwwe
Sorry for the dad joke, but these really do help as mnemonic devices when you’re learning Arabic. The similar sounds and associations can help words stick.
For hiyye, notice that it begins with the same h sound as the other third-person pronouns, but the -iyye sound tells you that it means she or feminine it.
Practice them together:
huwwe, hiyye, humme — هو، هي، هم — he, she, they
As you say huwwe, gesture toward an imaginary man.
As you say hiyye, gesture toward an imaginary woman.
As you say humme, gesture toward a group that you are talking about.

blocks.heading: Practice Them in Sequence
paragraphs: Memory tricks can help, but the best way to learn the pronouns is to say them aloud repeatedly in their three groups:
ana, iḥna | أنا، إحنا
inta, intī, intu | إنتَ، إنتي، إنتو
huwwe, hiyye, humme | هو، هي، هم
Use the gestures each time. Point to yourself, address imaginary people, and then gesture toward people you are talking about.
Do not try to translate every word slowly in your head. Practice the groups until their rhythm begins to feel natural:
1st Person: ana, iḥna — 2nd Person: inta, intī, intu — 3rd Person: huwwe, hiyye, humme
Say everything out loud. Repetition is your friend.

These pronouns will later combine with many other structures you’ll learn throughout this book, so it’s important to master them now. Once they become automatic, you’ll find that building longer sentences is much easier.

blocks.heading: Special Note — Connecting Ideas (و)
blocks.text: Linking ideas in Arabic is fairly easy. We often use و (w-), which means "and," to connect words and phrases. In Levantine Arabic, it is often pronounced like “w-,” “wi-,” or “u-,” and it attaches directly to the word that follows with no space. We will look at other conjunctions such as "but" and "or" later, but for now this small word is enough to start building connected sentences.

items.en: He is Ahmad and she is Sara.
I am Mohammad and you are Layla.

blocks.heading: 1.4 Common Names
paragraphs: Before we move on, let's take a quick look at some common names. This is something that often gets neglected in Arabic learning, but it comes up constantly in real life. If you travel to Jordan, Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, or anywhere in the Levant, you will hear names like these all the time.
You are also going to see them throughout this book in examples, drills, and conversations.

Learn to recognize them early, and practice saying them out loud. Names help the language feel more real and less abstract. Instead of only working with pronouns, you can start connecting the grammar to actual people.

blocks.heading: Putting It All Together
paragraphs: By this point, you have already begun building a foundation in Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic. You may not know many grammar rules yet—and that is completely okay. At this stage, the goal is to become familiar with the sound, rhythm, and natural flow of the language: how common phrases feel when people say them, how greetings and responses fit together, and how everyday exchanges move from one person to the next.

Rather than trying to analyze every word or memorize every rule immediately, begin getting comfortable with the overall feel of Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic. Listen for recurring sounds, notice familiar patterns, and allow the language to become more natural each time you see it, hear it, and say it aloud.
So far, you have practiced how to:
• Greet someone and return a greeting
• Use common everyday expressions
• Ask someone how they are and respond politely
• Introduce yourself and identify someone else
• Use common names and simple subject pronouns
• Ask basic questions using words such as “who,” “what,” “where,” and “how”
• Put familiar words and phrases together into short, meaningful sentences

You are not simply memorizing separate words. You are beginning to recognize how small pieces of language connect: a greeting can lead to a question, a question can lead to an introduction, and an introduction can become a real conversation.

On the next page, you will see a short story and dialogue that puts what you have learned into a natural, real-life context. You are not expected to understand every word right away. Look for the greetings, pronouns, names, question words, and expressions you already know. Use the pictures and the situation to help you understand the overall meaning, and read the dialogue aloud to get used to its rhythm.

Every chapter in this book will include a story and dialogue like this one. These scenes are where the language begins to come alive: they show how individual words, phrases, questions, and responses work together when people actually speak. As you move forward, the stories and dialogues will gradually become longer and more detailed. For now, focus on recognizing what you know, noticing how the pieces fit together, and becoming comfortable with the sound and flow of everyday Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic.

blocks.heading: Taha’s Café
paragraphs: Aaron and Walaa have just arrived in Amman after a long trip from the United States. Still carrying their suitcases, they enter a warm neighborhood café, where they meet the owner, Taha. As they greet one another, they talk about how they are doing, where Aaron and Walaa are from, and what they would like to order.

This dialogue brings together many of the greetings, pronouns, question words, introductions, and everyday expressions you have already practiced. You may notice a few new words or ideas from upcoming chapters—that is intentional. In real life, you will not always know every word in a conversation, but you can still understand a great deal by focusing on what you recognize, following the speakers, and using the situation to help you.

For now, do not worry about memorizing or analyzing every unfamiliar word. Those new pieces will be introduced soon. Instead, listen for familiar phrases, notice how questions and answers connect, and read the dialogue aloud to become more comfortable with the sound, rhythm, and natural flow of Southern Levantine Arabic.

Afterward, you will see the same conversation again in a comic format without English translations. Then you will complete a short drill in which you recreate the translations, helping you check your understanding and see how much Arabic you can already use.

blocks.heading: Dialogue Discussion — Taha’s Café
paragraphs: Aaron and Walaa have just arrived in Amman, and their first stop is a neighborhood café. Taha welcomes them in, asks a few questions, and takes their coffee order.

There are several expressions in this conversation that are worth discussing because they come up constantly in everyday Arabic. Some have straightforward English equivalents, while others make more sense when you understand how they’re used.

blocks.heading: السَّلام عليكم — Peace be upon you
paragraphs: Taha begins with:
Aaron and Walaa respond:

This is one of the most recognizable greetings in Arabic, and the one you learned at the beginning of this chapter. Although it has religious origins, you’ll hear it in many ordinary social situations.
Notice that the response reverses the wording of the greeting. This is a fixed exchange, so it’s worth learning both parts together.

blocks.heading: كيفكم؟ — How are you all?
paragraphs: Taha then asks:
The ending ـكم (-kum) tells us that Taha is speaking to more than one person.
Aaron and Walaa answer:

items.en: We’re well, thank God. And you?

paragraphs: Here, منيحين is the plural form, since Aaron and Walaa are answering together. They could’ve also answered with the broken plural مْناح, and it would’ve been correct as well—but we’ll get into that later.
Notice how they return the question with وإنت؟. In a conversation, you don’t always need to repeat the entire question. A simple “And you?” is often enough.

blocks.heading: إنتو من وين؟ — Where are you all from?
paragraphs: Taha asks:
Aaron responds:

Notice how Aaron answers in two steps. He first tells Taha his nationality, then adds a more specific place of origin: Texas. You can answer the same way when someone asks where you’re from—give your nationality, then add your state, city, or another place that tells the listener more. The second part follows the familiar min + place pattern.

blocks.heading: Keeping the Conversation Going
paragraphs: After introducing themselves, Aaron and Walaa exchange a couple of polite expressions with Taha. These are particularly useful when meeting someone for the first time.

blocks.heading: تشرّفنا — Nice to meet you
paragraphs: Taha says:
Aaron and Walaa respond:
The word شَرَف relates to honor. Literally, the response expresses that the honor belongs to us.
You don’t need to translate these expressions word for word every time you hear them. Think of them as a natural pair used during introductions.

blocks.heading: صاحِب هالقَهْوة — The owner of this café
paragraphs: Taha introduces himself:

items.en: My name is Taha, and I’m the owner of this café.

paragraphs: The word صاحِب is interesting in colloquial Arabic. It can mean “friend,” but it can also mean “owner,” depending on the context.
Here, Taha is telling Aaron and Walaa that he owns the café.
You’ll also notice هالـ attached to قَهْوة. It’s a common way of saying “this” in everyday Levantine Arabic. We’ll examine that pattern more closely in Chapter 2.

blocks.heading: بِدْنا — We want
paragraphs: When Taha asks what they’d like, Aaron responds:

items.en: We want two cups of plain coffee.

paragraphs: بِدْنا means “we want.” You’ll learn how to use بِدّ with different pronouns in Chapter 4. For now, recognize it as a useful expression when ordering.
Aaron uses فنجانين for “two cups.” This gives the order a warmer, more traditional feel. You may also hear كاستين, a more general way to say “two cups.”
The word سادة describes coffee served plain, without sugar or other additions. So قهوة سادة means plain, unsweetened coffee.
